item.title: REVIEW: McAfee Total Protection for Mac Review: Capable Cross-Platform Security
item.description:
Source: PCMag
MacOS was designed with security in mind from the start, while Windows security was bolted on later. That's one reason there’s more malware aimed at Windows systems than there is at Macs, but that doesn’t mean Macs are immune. You still need antivirus protection for your Macs, and the cross-platform McAfee Total Protection comes from a fairly well-known name. It offers solid protection, but its feature set for Macs is limited compared with the Windows edition, and the antivirus testing labs don’t vouch for its efficacy. Bitdefender Antivirus and Norton 360 Deluxe, by contrast, hold perfect or near-perfect scores from three labs that test Mac antivirus software, so they remain our Editors’ Choice winners for protecting your Mac against malware. You used to pay $64.99 per year to install McAfee AntiVirus Plus on every device in your household, including your Macs. That product is no longer available for macOS, so those who want McAfee protection for their Macs should start with McAfee Total Protection, reviewed here. It’s true that McAfee Antivirus still exists, but its sun is setting. It only protects one PC, with no cross-platform support or volume discounts. McAfee doesn’t even sell it, leaving that task to third parties. And while McAfee Total Protection and McAfee+ got a thorough makeover this fall, the antivirus was left behind. I can’t recommend McAfee Antivirus anymore. If you’re a McAfee enthusiast, you should go for one of the suite products. Pricing for McAfee Total Protection starts at $89.99 per year to protect a single Mac. That’s quite a bit more than most standalone macOS antivirus tools, which does make sense since this is a cross-platform security suite. Only Intego One costs as much as McAfee. A three-license annual McAfee subscription costs $99.99 and lets you install protection on your macOS, Windows, iOS, Android, and ChromeOS devices. As with the single-license tier, that price is quite high compared with most standalone antivirus utilities for macOS, though at $114.99 for three licenses, Intego is even higher. Malwarebytes Premium Security, Panda Dome Essential, and Total Defense Essential Anti-Virus cost much less, $59.99 per year for three licenses, while Bitdefender and Webroot Essentials cost $69.99. A three-pack of ClamXAV goes for just $29.95. The most logical comparison is McAfee against Norton 360 Deluxe. Norton is also a cross-platform suite that supports macOS, Windows, and Android. At the five-license tier, Norton costs $5 more than McAfee’s $ 119.99-per-year plan. In addition to their other security features, both apps offer VPN protection for five devices with no bandwidth or server limits. A five-license subscription is as high as you go with McAfee Total Protection unless you jump ship from McAfee to a third-party supplier. Retailers like Best Buy and Amazon sometimes offer an unlimited-license package for $149.99 per year, usually with a steep discount the first year. However, you can get unlimited licenses for the advanced McAfee+ suite directly from McAfee at the same $149.99 per year. At higher tiers, McAfee+ adds a comprehensive identity protection system, much like the one you get with Norton 360 with LifeLock Select. Of course, you can also get antivirus protection for your Mac for no charge by choosing Avast One Free for Mac, AVG AntiVirus, or Avira Free Antivirus. Most Mac users keep their macOS installations up to date. Norton recognizes this, supporting only the current macOS and two previous versions. At present, that means Golden Gate, Tahoe, and Sequoia. Webroot’s plan is similar, but it goes back three previous versions, adding Sonoma. McAfee supports all of those plus macOS 10.13 (Ventura). For those stuck running an older macOS version, perhaps due to older hardware, Bitdefender, ClamXav, or K7 AntiVirus may be a better choice, with support dating back to 10.10 (Yosemite). As with many cross-platform security programs, McAfee’s installation process starts online. You log in or create your account, enter your registration code, and download the installer to your Mac. During installation, McAfee offers a Virus Protection Pledge. This pledge means that if a malware attack gets past an existing McAfee installation, McAfee's trained malware experts will remotely connect to your computer and fix the problem. If the experts can't fix the problem, McAfee will refund your purchase price (but isn’t liable for any ancillary damage from the malware). To get this pledge from McAfee, you must make your own automatic renewal pledge, which seems reasonable. You get a similar pledge and a similar automatic-renewal requirement with Norton and ZoneAlarm Extreme Security. As noted, your license lets you install McAfee on your Windows devices, as well as your iOS, ChromeOS, and Android devices. Please read my review of McAfee Total Protection for full details on what you get with the other platforms. Briefly, the Windows edition has features—including a firewall, a tracker blocker, and a file shredder—that are not available on the Mac. The Android edition offers features beyond antivirus with a strong focus on the scam protection system, and the iOS edition (as expected) is relatively limited in its feature set. The last time McAfee’s security apps got a makeover, the Mac edition was left out. With the current change, it’s very, very similar to the Windows version. As on Windows, McAfee’s home page always displays the next action you need to take for improved security. If you’ve handled all pending tasks, you get a congratulatory green panel reading “All clear, safety superstar.” Below this panel are three large buttons labeled Quick actions. These serve to launch an antivirus scan, turn the VPN on or off, or extend McAfee protection to more devices. Also, under Windows, a menu of icons runs down the left side. Icons for Home, Protection, and Protection summary occupy the top. Safety alerts, Settings, and Sign out appear at the bottom of this menu. Clicking Protection from the left-side menu opens the app’s protection page. This page has four tabs: Devices, Personal info, Scams, and Finances. The Finances tab isn’t relevant to McAfee Total Protection; it applies to McAfee+. Personal info and Scams work exactly as they do under Windows. That leaves the Devices tab, which is dominated by a statistics panel showing the number of devices you’ve protected with McAfee as well as the number of threats resolved across all those devices. Below the stats panel, you’ll find three buttons: Secure VPN, Web Protection, and Antivirus. Just as in the Windows edition, these let you use and configure the named features. However, the Windows edition includes four more buttons representing Smart Scan, Firewall, File Shredder, and Tracker Remover. These four aren’t features of the Mac edition. Longtime McAfee trackers will note that yes, the previous Mac version did include a firewall component. The teams of testers and researchers at independent antivirus testing labs can devote significant resources to evaluating and rating antivirus tools. I follow five such labs for my Windows antivirus reviews, three of which also release regular reports on Mac antivirus. Since my hands-on testing setup, developed over many years, is entirely Windows-based, those sets of lab results become especially important to my Mac antivirus reviews. When I first evaluated McAfee's macOS antivirus nearly 15 years ago, it had AV-Comparatives certification, with perfect detection of Mac malware and excellent detection of Windows malware. McAfee hasn’t appeared in this lab's test results in the last few years, nor has it been included in AV-Test Institute's test reports. G Data Antivirus, Malwarebytes, Sophos Home Premium, Trend Micro Antivirus, and Webroot are among the numerous others that lack recent lab scores. If you want to choose an antivirus for your Mac based on top lab test results, look to Bitdefender, ESET Cyber Security, or Norton. These are the only apps with scores from all three labs, and they’ve got a fine bunch of scores. All three took 100% from SE Labs. ESET and Norton reached 99.9% with AV-Comparatives, with Bitdefender at 99.0%. Bitdefender and Norton scored a perfect 18 points with AV-Test Institute, while ESET came close at 17.5 points. Like most Mac antivirus tools, McAfee aims to detect and remove any Windows malware it encounters. True, malware written for Windows won’t run under macOS, but you wouldn’t want your Mac to become a carrier. To check this feature’s effectiveness, I challenged McAfee by mounting a USB drive containing the samples I use for Windows antivirus testing. My collection runs the gamut from potentially unwanted applications (PUAs) to pernicious ransomware. On Windows, it’s clear that McAfee checks programs for malware on download and on launch. For this Mac test, I simply scanned the USB drive. McAfee detected and quarantined 90% of samples, placing it in the top quarter among current Mac antivirus apps. Webroot tops the current list, with 99% detection of Windows malware. Intego, Surfshark, and Sophos came in higher than McAfee, but it beat all the rest. Most of the Mac antivirus utilities I've evaluated offer at least two kinds of scans: a quick scan that looks for active malware and checks the most likely areas for infestation, and a full scan that covers your entire computer. Most supplement these with a custom scan of user-specified locations. The antivirus page of McAfee’s Windows edition offers these three familiar choices, but on the Mac you get only the quick and custom scans. That’s a change from past versions. My McAfee contact confirmed the change, saying, “We know that full scans on Macs can take a considerable amount of time without necessarily providing much additional protection against today's threats. That's why we focused on giving customers effective, practical ways to stay protected without adding unnecessary steps.” In theory, once you’ve rooted out any lurking malware with a full scan, you should be able to rely on real-time protection to handle any new problems. Even so, a regularly scheduled scan can’t help but enhance your protection. On Windows, you can set McAfee to scan weekly, every two weeks, or monthly. Given the Mac edition has dropped the full scan, it’s no surprise that scheduling is also absent. If you're a nefarious web design expert rather than a malicious coder, phishing is your perfect crime. All you need to do is create a website that precisely replicates the appearance of a sensitive site and then find a way to direct hapless victims to your site. When an unsuspecting user logs in to your fake site, you grab their credentials and take over the account. You can now use those credentials to, say, log into the victim's bank and drain all the funds or take over an email account and use it to reset passwords for all the victim’s other accounts. For my Windows antiphishing tests, I use a small utility that lets me launch a suspected phishing URL and click a button to indicate whether the antivirus blocked it, missed it, or the page wasn't a proper phishing attempt after all. I use the utility to launch the same collection of URLs against the phishing protection built into Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, and on a system protected by the antivirus under test. When it's a macOS antivirus, testing phishing protection is a manual process that involves a lot of copy-pasting and button-mashing. I tested McAfee’s Windows and macOS editions simultaneously, both in Chrome. Not surprisingly, the test results on the two platforms came in identical. On both macOS and Windows, McAfee blocked the browser from 100% of verified fraud attempts. The macOS editions of AVG, Avira, Norton, and Webroot also achieved 100% detection in their latest tests. The WebAdvisor component helps steer your browsing away from malicious and fraudulent pages, and it works just as well on macOS as it does on Windows. It also marks up links in search results, red-flagging those that would be dangerous to visit. By default, it only does so if you use McAfee’s own search engine. To remove that limitation, click the WebAdvisor toolbar button, click the gear-shaped icon for settings, and scroll down. Choose the option that says “Tell me if a search result is safe in any search engine." WebAdvisor also marks up links in social media posts on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, Reddit, X/Twitter, and YouTube. Social markup is enabled by default, so you don’t need to change anything to get it. If you want full-scale identity theft remediation from McAfee, you must subscribe to one of the higher-priced tiers of McAfee+. Even so, McAfee Total Protection scans the dark web for your personal information and alerts you when your data appears in a breach. This feature isn’t tied to a specific device, though you can manage your personal info and view alerts from any of your devices. Whether on a Mac or a Windows PC, click Protection in the left-side menu, then click the Personal info tab, and click the panel labeled Identity monitoring. Out of the box, McAfee checks the email address associated with your account to see whether it has been exposed in any data breaches. You can click the Monitored info tab to add quite a few other elements of personal data for monitoring: - Bank accounts (10) - Credit cards (10) - Date of birth (1) - Driver’s licenses (2) - Email addresses (10) - Health IDs (2) - Passports (2) - Phone numbers (10) - Social Security number (1) - Tax IDs (2) - Usernames (10) I go into more detail on this feature in my main McAfee Total Protection review. Suffice it to say that McAfee reports when it finds any of this information exposed in a data breach. It’s up to you to take any appropriate action, such as changing your password. Once you’ve reviewed a result, you can acknowledge it, thereby removing it from the active list. Reviewing breaches from the list and marking them as handled raises your protection score. But where do you see that score? In the previous version, you could click a Protection Score icon, which would open the online protection center and display your score as a figure on a scale from 0 to 1,000. With the latest McAfee version, you must log in to your account online and click the Protection Score icon in the left-side menu. Whatever your score may be, McAfee offers several actions you can take to raise it. Hey, we all want a better score, right? McAfee’s own studies show that when presented with such recommendations, more than half of users take action to improve their security. The McAfee portal is also the place to install or manage the True Key password manager. True Key works just the same on macOS as on Windows. Please read my full review of McAfee Total Protection for details about True Key. This suite protects your data on your Mac, but when that data heads out to the wild internet, it becomes vulnerable. To secure your data in transit, you should run your connection through a VPN. The connection is encrypted between your device and the VPN server, so even if the Wi-Fi network you’re using is compromised, nobody can access your data. A VPN also masks your IP address, making it impossible for the websites you visit to determine your location based on that address. With a one-license McAfee suite subscription, you quite logically get the ability to apply VPN protection on one device. Three- or five-license subscriptions expand your VPN protection to allow three or five simultaneous connections. As with its Windows counterpart, the VPN is integrated right into the suite. Connecting through any VPN server, even one that’s right next to you, gets you the advantages described above. But running your traffic through a server in another country can also unblock region-locked content. And of course, when you’re traveling, it’s convenient to have the option to connect with a nearby server. Some VPNs let you choose a particular server or type of server in the city of your choice. Others just let you choose the city (smaller countries may have only one city to choose from). McAfee’s server choices are more limited—all you can do is choose from a list of four dozen countries. If you choose the United States, your server could be anywhere, from Humptulips, WA, to Okeefenokee, FL. Once you’ve selected a country, engaging VPN protection is as simple as flipping the switch to On. By default, the VPN is active only when you manually enable it. You can set it to automatically engage any time you connect to a network or limit auto-connect to Wi-Fi networks. For fine-tuning, you can tell it to skip VPN protection on known, trusted Wi-Fi networks. When last reviewed, McAfee on the Mac did not offer split tunneling (the ability to divert less sensitive traffic outside the VPN’s protection), nor did it have the Safe Reconnect feature, sometimes called a kill switch. In the current edition, it closely matches the Windows edition's feature set, including both of these features. McAfee’s VPN is very easy to use, and it comes without the painful bandwidth limitations imposed by some competing suites. It adds significant value to this security suite. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. McAfee Total Protection for Mac doesn’t match the security suite features of its Windows equivalent, though the current edition comes closer than in the past. On the plus side, it includes VPN protection, a system to flag scam messages, and the effective WebAdvisor browser extension. Independent testing labs don’t vouch for it, though. In the Mac antivirus realm, our Editors’ Choice award goes to Bitdefender Antivirus and Norton 360 Deluxe. Both have earned perfect and near-perfect scores from three independent testing labs, and both offer an impressive array of security features for Macs. STILL ON THE FENCE? - ● The Best Mac Antivirus Software for 2026 When the IBM PC was new, I served as the president of the San Francisco PC User Group for three years. That’s how I met PCMag’s editorial team, who brought me on board in 1986. In the years since that fateful meeting, I’ve become PCMag’s expert on security, privacy, and identity protection, putting antivirus tools, security suites, and all kinds of security software through their paces. Before my current security gig, I supplied PCMag readers with tips and solutions on using popular applications, operating systems, and programming languages in my "User to User" and "Ask Neil" columns, which began in 1990 and ran for almost 20 years. Along the way, I wrote more than 40 utility articles, as well as Delphi Programming for Dummies and six other books covering DOS, Windows, and programming. I also reviewed thousands of products of all kinds, ranging from early Sierra Online adventure games to AOL’s precursor Q-Link. In the early 2000s, I turned my focus to security and the growing antivirus industry. After years of working with antivirus, I’m known throughout the security industry as an expert on evaluating antivirus tools. I serve as an advisory board member for the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO), an international nonprofit group dedicated to coordinating and improving testing of anti-malware solutions.

item.title: SALES: Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border. Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.) Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time. Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing. The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow. Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character. Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards. Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home. Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure. Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here. Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.

item.title: REVIEW: Edifier MR3 Review: Affordable Speakers That Punch Above Their Weight
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Edifier had a hit on its hands with the powerful and economical MR5, which remains one of our top computer speaker recommendations. The company has now also introduced a more compact and affordable option with the MR3. These miss out on the MR5's three-way driver arrangement but still have the looks and much of the same functionality. At $149, these speakers aren’t terribly expensive, but they still deliver sound quality that rivals the JBL 104-BT. On top of that, they’re a bit more flexible with easy EQ customization, offer built-in and in-app tools to compensate for room acoustics, and they’re just prettier to look at, too. With all that in mind, they earn our Editors’ Choice recommendation for best affordable computer speakers. The MR3 speakers blend the qualities of studio monitors with those of more standard desktop speakers. They have cleanly assembled MDF cabinets sitting at just 4.94 inches wide and 8.66 inches tall. The right active speaker measures 7.28 inches deep, while the passive speaker is a bit smaller at 6.92 inches. They have a combined weight of just under 8.5 pounds. At those dimensions, the MR3 speakers are a fair bit smaller than the Fluance Ai41, though not quite as small as the JBL 104-BT. Still, they’re very desk-friendly, especially using standard speaker wire to pair them and integrating the power supply into the main speaker so a wall wart isn’t required. The MR3 squeezes in 3.5-inch mid-low drivers, 1-inch silk-dome tweeters, and rear ports. Each speaker delivers 18 watts RMS. Edifier gives the setup a stylish flourish with a carbon-fiber-style cone material and a bronze-colored cap that matches the bronze volume dial. The speakers sit on small rubber feet to dampen vibrations, but you don’t get angled stands. To make up for the lack of stands, the tweeters have dimpled waveguides that attempt to more evenly disperse the sound. The Edifier MR3 can fit into different setups with a combination of stereo RCA, 3.5mm AUX, and Bluetooth 5.4 inputs for regular listening, and quarter-inch balanced TRS inputs for use with an audio mixer or digital audio workstation. There’s no dedicated subwoofer output, so if you’re planning to work with a subwoofer, you’ll need to get a studio-style one that can pass along sound to the speakers down the line. Although most of the inputs are on the rear, Edifier places the AUX on the front for easy access and adds a 3.5mm output jack to make switching to headphones easy. The Bluetooth connection is unusually tame for an Edifier speaker. Many in the brand support LDAC for high-resolution wireless audio, but the MR3 is limited to SBC, not even reaching AAC, resulting in flatter audio performance over Bluetooth. Multipoint is supported, and switching between playback sources was quick. Wired audio sources can also play simultaneously with Bluetooth sources. To help manage the sound, the speakers feature acoustic tuning dials on the rear to boost or cut frequencies by up to 6dB. The high knob controls frequencies over 10kHz and the low knob handles frequencies below 125Hz. This can help counteract room acoustics that impact the sound that reaches you. There’s further control available in Edifier’s app. The front of the main speaker has a notched volume dial that can also be pressed. It doesn’t have hard limits, instead keeping a nearby indicator light solid to indicate when it has reached maximum or minimum volume. This does mean there’s no telling whether you’re at 10% or 90% volume until you play some sound, so you’ll want to check your source devices first to avoid loud surprises. Tapping the power button cycles through EQ settings, and the indicator light changes color accordingly (red for monitor, green for music, white for custom). There’s also a Bluetooth pairing button at the back. The Edifier MR3 uses the same Edifier Connex app as the rest of the brand’s speakers and headphones use. With this model, the app's features are fairly bare-bones but useful. It lets you clearly select between Monitor and Music EQ settings rather than relying on the main speaker’s indicator light to know which is selected. You can create a custom EQ setting with nine bands to adjust by up to 3dB in either direction in 0.5dB increments. The app also provides extra acoustic tuning controls. You can create a low cutoff point from 20-100Hz and slopes from -6 to -24dB/octave. There’s an Acoustic Space setting that helps tame the bass-boosting effects of speaker placement near corners or walls. Finally, there’s a toggle called Desktop Control that aims to mitigate frequency boosting caused by sound waves reflecting off desktops or other surfaces near the speaker drivers. Beyond this, the app’s functionality is limited. It manages firmware updates and includes a user manual, but it doesn’t provide access to Bluetooth Multipoint control or additional codecs. On the bright side, no account is needed to get up and running. The Edifier MR3 speakers have pleasant and clean sound, though with some clear limitations in the low end. In The Knife’s “Silent Shout,” the speakers give a bold presentation of the bass triplets, and the shaker has some brilliant texture in the high end, but when the sub-bass quarters are introduced, they fall a bit flat. To be clear, they hit hard with a pronounced attack, but they’re meant to roll off into a lower frequency, and the MR3 can’t quite follow, resulting in more of a sub-bass smack than intended. The speakers render the rest of the track brilliantly. They show no hints of distortion even while pumping out the volume—easily enough for small and medium rooms. The synth melody is rich and readily rolls back and forth between mellow and biting with wonderful texture. The cymbals sound lifelike, with ample high-end presence, and the track's many subtle nuances come through. Both vocal harmonies come through clearly with clean phasing effects. Kendrick Lamar’s “Loyalty” better shows the limitations of the MR3 low-end. The chorus introduces a deep, sub-bass line, and the MR3 can’t reproduce almost any of these notes. There are a few octaves for accent that come through, and thankfully the speakers don’t play them too loudly or abruptly (a lot of speakers I’ve tested seem to burp these notes in awful fashion), but this still makes it clear how much a subwoofer is needed for full depth. The rest of the track is otherwise excellent, with the drums hitting hard and cymbals ringing out clearly. Lamar’s and Rihanna’s vocals are bright and clear in the phantom center. Bill Callahan’s “Drover” plays into the MR3’s effective range, letting them give a strong showing. Their lack of low-end actually helps subdue the constant patter of the kick drum, which is just at the edge of their response range. Callahan’s baritone vocals, meanwhile, come through rich and full in the phantom center. The speakers muster clear stereo separation, letting the electric guitar and fiddle sweep in from the sides for great effect. The instrumentation gets a lively presentation thanks to crisp high-end that gives plenty of texture without becoming grating. The MR3's strong high-end capabilities help with orchestral music like John Adams’ The Gospel According to the Other Mary. With rich orchestration, every little bit helps, and the high-end provides more texture to the instruments so they can better stand out from one another. The vocals are clear and largely centered. The limited low-end still cuts out some of the instrumentation, which can go quite low. The section “Lazarus Rises From the Dead” has a considerable swell from near silence that starts in the deep bass ranges and is completely missed by the MR3. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. All told, the MR3 are a great set of desktop speakers for the price. They put out a ton of volume for their size and deliver largely flat EQ without overemphasizing any band. They face some limitations without a subwoofer that are fairly common for speakers of this kind, but their audio performance at the remaining frequencies is great. Next to the JBL 104-BT, they may not have as much bass depth, but they manage their bass better and avoid distortion. They also offer better room control and customization through an app. All that in an affordable package is enough to give the Edifier MR3 our Editors’ Choice Award for best budget-priced computer speakers. There’s nothing like the excitement of an international trip. Whether you’re revisiting a favourite destination or stepping off the plane into a new country, the thrill of landing somewhere far from home never gets old. However, that good mood can quickly sour if you find yourself at a hotel or Airbnb with no way to plug in your devices. After all, our phone reliance is often high on the road, from using it to get around, find things to do and even communicate in different languages. That's where a reliable travel adaptor comes in. Read on for my picks of the best travel adaptors for your next international trip, so you can keep your phone, Kindle, iPad, smartwatches and other gear properly charged up. What's the difference between a travel adaptor and a converter? A travel adaptor simply changes the shape of your plug to fit into a different socket. A converter changes the voltage so it is compatible with your device. There are different voltage standards worldwide – European countries use 220V, while the US uses 110-120V. If your device isn’t dual-voltage and you only use an adaptor in a country with a different voltage, you risk ruining it. What type of adaptor do I need for international travel? The type of adaptor you’ll need for international travel depends on several factors, like the types of devices you're bringing along and the shape of the sockets you’ll be using during your trip. item.title: REVIEW: TCL 27C2A Pro 27-inch QD-Mini LED 4K gaming monitor review: Extreme color and brightness
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Stand issues aside, the TCL 27C2A Pro delivers a colorful and bright image with fine pixel density and smooth gaming performance. With broad contrast and vivid color, it’s the next best thing to a premium OLED. - +Extremely bright with broad contrast and vivid color - +Very accurate in color gamut preset modes - +Excellent video processing with smooth panel response - +Extras like LED lights, USB ports, KVM and internal speakers Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. You’ve probably heard TCL’s name associated with jumbo TVs sold in big-box stores, but it also makes a line of gaming monitors that offer excellent performance for the money. It’s also one of the few companies putting effort into Mini LED panels where others have gone all-in with OLED. Mini LED delivers the brightest imagery you can buy among the best gaming monitors, with HDR peaks of 2,000 nits or more. TCL’s 27C2A Pro is such a panel, with an honest 2,000 nits from a 3% window in HDR mode and 650 nits full field for SDR. It also sports a full-array local dimming (FALD) backlight with 2,304 zones, which delivers tremendous contrast. A Quantum Dot layer pushes the color gamut past 100% of DCI-P3. And a set of accurate picture modes promise precise color rendering. It’s speedy too, with 160 Hz in 4K and 320 Hz in FHD resolution, with available overdrive and MPRT backlight strobing. This fully loaded package can be yours for $600 as I write this. Let’s take a look. The 27C2A Pro’s core tech is an IPS variant TCL calls HFS Shoot. It combines an ultra-bright FALD backlight with Quantum Dot color and very quick response. Native resolution is 4K 3840x2160 pixels for a density of 163ppi. This is about as fine as it gets unless you move up to 5K or more. And those panels are still quite rare and expensive. Brightness is honestly reported here, with my tests matching TCL’s claims. I saw almost 650 nits from a full white field pattern in SDR mode with the dimming turned off. HDR ran that up to almost 1,700 nits when I measured a 25% window with dimming on High. At that setting, I couldn’t measure the black levels at all. With 2,304 dimming zones, you won’t see any halo artifacts like panels with just a few hundred zones. The Quantum Dot layer delivers just over 100% of the DCI-P3 gamut. You also get accurate picture modes with presets for DCI-P3, sRGB, Rec.709, and Adobe RGB, which is something rarely found outside the professional realm. Accuracy is superb with little to no need for calibration. I found similarly good performance in HDR mode, where you can adjust grayscale tracking and brightness if you wish. The 27C2A Pro offers premium gaming too, with 160 Hz in 4K and 320 Hz in FHD resolution with a dual-mode switch. And there’s precise overdrive, Adaptive-Sync, and MPRT backlight strobing. This is one of the few monitors that lets you use all its video processing options at the same time. You can have MPRT, Adaptive-Sync, and overdrive all active at once. Styling is outside the norm as well, with a white aesthetic for the stand and panel’s backside. LED lighting shines in the back with two large bracket shapes that show an array of colors and effects. There are gaming aids like reticles, timers, and a frame rate indicator. And you get a full complement of I/O ports with HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, and a USB-C, plus USB for your peripherals. The 27C2A Pro ships in blocks of crumbly foam in its three main parts: base, upright, and panel. They assemble without tools. Under the snap-on fulcrum is a 100mm VESA mount with fasteners included if you'd rather use an arm, and you might want to after you read the next section of this review. The power supply is an external brick, and you get cables for DisplayPort, HDMI, USB-A/B, and USB-C. I said the 27C2A Pro is a white monitor, but from the front, everything is black except the base. This is good for distraction-free use, especially in low-light situations where you want to stay focused on the image. There’s plenty of white plastic in the back, though, on the stand and on the panel. The back features ventilation across the top and two large LED banks shaped like reversed parentheses. The shapes are angular with soft corners and no sharp edges. The screen has a flush bezel 9mm thick on the top and sides with a 15mm strip across the bottom. All you see there is a tiny TCL logo. The control joystick is underneath the center and is backlit. The stand offers full ergonomics with 5/15 degrees tilt, 20 degrees swivel, and a 90-degree portrait mode. The height range is 4.8 inches. This was my only complaint about the 27C2A Pro. Though the base and upright are solid together, the panel’s fulcrum point is very small and wobbly, which makes positioning it difficult. If you game intensely and have your keyboard on the desk, it will jiggle a bit. Up and under the center is a well-stocked I/O panel with one DisplayPort 1.4, two HDMI 2.1, and a USB-C with 90 watts of power. You also get one upstream and two downstream USB 3.0 ports. There is a pair of five-watt internal speakers, and you get a 3.5mm headphone jack. In 4K resolution, the 27C2A Pro’s OSD is very small. It was hard to read the tiny text unless I got up close. The FHD version is larger, of course. Press the joystick and click left to summon it. Player mode refers to the nine picture modes you see in the first photo above. All you need is the default one, Standard, and I’ll tell you why in a moment. Moving on to Game Settings, the 27C2A Pro has every video processing option currently available for an LCD panel. The overdrive has three speeds, with fast being the best. MPRT-Plus (backlight strobe) has two levels, which correspond to pulse width. The higher one cuts brightness by around 50%, but you can easily compensate with the brightness slider because there’s more than enough luminance headroom. You can use both with Adaptive-Sync if you wish, which is something very few monitors can do. I found the best motion quality with overdrive on Fast and Adaptive-Sync engaged. MPRT reduces motion blur to almost nothing but introduces a slight phasing artifact, so I didn’t use it for my gaming tests. Also in this menu are a set of aiming points, timers, and controls for the LED lighting. The Display menu starts with Local Dimming and its three levels. Standard barely does anything, only increasing contrast to around 1,800:1. Medium and High are more aggressive, and they shut off the backlight completely at light level zero for theoretically infinite contrast. Dimming is available for both SDR and HDR content. In the Color menu, you’ll find color temp presets and a gamut selector. It offers sRGB, Rec.709, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. All are very accurate, more so than the Original option, in fact. You’ll see how this works in my tests on page four. The 27C2A Pro is a very accurate monitor when set up correctly. The remainder of the OSD is focused on conveniences like PIP/PBP, KVM options, OSD controls, and the like. If you want to reset everything to factory defaults, that option is in the Settings menu. I was initially disappointed with the 27C2A Pro during my first round of tests. It comes set to Standard mode, Original color space, warm color temp, and gamma 1. Gamma and grayscale measured well, but color tracking was a bit wonky. Luckily, you can select any of the available gamuts, sRGB, Rec.709, DCI-P3, or Adobe RGB, and get much better accuracy with near-perfect gamma and grayscale. I made small tweaks to the RGB sliders, and that was it. My settings are below. In HDR mode, you get two presets, Display and Cinema. Their color is the same, but the EOTF curves are slightly different. My pick was Display, and with that, you get RGB sliders and a brightness control. You can also change the local dimming, though I recommend High for the deepest blacks and best contrast. Gaming on the 27C2A Pro was a treat. I’m spoiled by premium OLEDs, but TCL has found a great combination of brightness, color, speed, and smoothness that mostly replicates that experience with an LCD panel. The only thing you won’t get is those infinite blacks, but the 27C2A Pro comes close with its 2,304 dimming zones and extremely bright highlights. You’ll see later in the test notes just how bright it can get, and that capability is used to full effect. I always set up review displays to 200 nits, and that was only a third of the 27C2A Pro’s SDR brightness range. I found that I could use its local dimming for both SDR and HDR content, which was nice. Often, there is only dimming for HDR. Color was also a strength, with vivid hues and excellent accuracy. I found some unusual behavior during initial tests, but once I discovered the secret, it was pro-level color all the way. Just pick the gamut you want and avoid the Original option in the OSD’s color space menu. My GeForce RTX 4090-equipped PC had no problem maintaining 160fps in 4K. I tried the FHD/320 Hz option and found that it worked fine and delivered that frame rate. Since the downscale is an exact multiple, the picture wasn’t as soft as you might expect. The dual-mode feature is a viable option for users with consoles or less stout video cards. I also noted that I could use overdrive and MPRT backlight strobing in concert with Adaptive-Sync. That’s something only a few high-end monitors offer, so it was nice to see from a $600 display. If you’re relegated to frame rates below 144 Hz, MPRT is a good option for eliminating motion blur. The overdrive on its own is also very effective at its middle setting, Fast. Lag was low enough that I didn’t perceive any delay in control response. Backgrounds and moving objects stayed sharp, and my inputs were instantly translated to action. The 27C2A Pro has that addictive quality that all fast and smooth monitors have. For productivity, the 27C2A Pro shines as a photo and graphics display. Its color modes include sRGB, Rec.709, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. That last one is a rarity outside the professional realm. They are spot-on, as you’ll see in my test results; no calibration needed. If you need a print reference monitor, this one qualifies. I also noted that the 27C2A Pro is a complete package with LED lighting, internal speakers, USB ports with KVM, and a slick white aesthetic. My only complaint is that the stand is too wobbly. The base and upright are solid, but the panel’s attachment point has some jiggle. I would probably spend some of the money I saved over an OLED on an arm. Takeaway: The 27C2A Pro is a complete package for gaming and productivity. It’s fast and smooth with excellent video processing and the ability to run Adaptive-Sync along with overdrive and backlight strobing. It’s colorful and sharp and has deep contrast thanks to 2,304 local dimming zones. It’s also much brighter than any OLED. It delivers tremendous bang for the buck.

item.title: SALES: REEF Made the Ultimate Do-It-All Sneaker
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
The REEF Del Mar is a versatile men’s sneaker designed for all-day comfort, easy step-in wear and everyday performance. (Photo: REEF x Outside) For over four decades, REEF has been powering adventures by the water with sandals, slides, and flip-flops that live up to the brand’s “Ridiculously Comfortable” promise. Now, thanks to the versatile Del Mar Sneaker, REEF is ensuring that you can stroll from the boardwalk to the boardroom in the same pair of shoes. Stylish, practical, and, of course, comfortable, the Del Mar is an everyday sneaker built for morning meetings, sunset sails, and everything in between. Think of the Del Mar as the opposite of the specialty shoe. The minds at REEF wanted a sneaker that broke down barriers: Why let athletic shoes have all the cushioned comfort? Why let dress shoes be the only ones that catch the eye? And why let a casual shoe be resigned to the weekend? The Del Mar aims to skip the split and give you a shoe for every part of your busy life, whether you’re hanging out or hustling. Its details and restrained pops of color give it enough polish for a meeting but still feel right at home at those weekend barbecues. Jack Crivici-Kramer, co-host of The Best One Yet podcast, put it simply: “They go with jeans, they go with khakis, they go with shorts…they might even go with a tuxedo.” So what’s actually under your foot that takes the Del Mar from “comfortable” to “Ridiculously Comfortable?” Several thoughtful elements combine to give this sneaker the kind of upgrade that elevates a shoe from a once-in-a-while wear to a daily driver. A rubber-infused foam midsole provides cushioning, a plush FlexCore insole adds support, and a heel gravity pod helps the shoe roll forward with each step. This combination makes the Del Mar feel springy rather than stiff, the kind of all-important element that’s missing from so many professional-ready footwear options. Corey Wilson, a photographer who’s constantly on his feet, sees the value in exactly that. “As a creative, every single day is different. I’m constantly in different environments; life’s constantly changing,” he says. “I need something that’s comfortable, something you can just slip on and just do so many different things with.” The engineered knit upper is what separates the Del Mar from other lifestyle sneakers; it flexes with your foot so you can move with confidence on bike commutes or long afternoon walks. Just as importantly, it breathes well enough to ensure that your feet won’t overheat. When you’re moving from an active setting to a more formal one, keeping cool is invaluable. The elastic lace option is where the knit does its best work. It fits closer to a sock than a sneaker and holds the foot without pinching, giving you a secure fit that feels as though it’s perfectly molded to your foot. The hands-free step-in is a convenient and comfortable way to get up and go. Meanwhile, standard laces come in the box if you’d rather tie your shoes for a more traditional look and fit. Because REEF was born by the water, the SoCal-based company also knows how much traction matters. The Del Mar has a grippy outsole with rubber pods at the toe and heel, thoughtfully placed where daily wear tends to concentrate. This unique design keeps the shoe’s weight down, too. That rubber is used only where it’s most essential for secure footing on slippery docks, wet streets, and freshly mopped office floors. You’ve got durability and security, all while the shoe maintains its light, carefree feel. As a brand that’s named for and constantly inspired by the ocean, REEF is committed to protecting coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them through sustainable practices and environmental partnerships. One way in which sustainability takes shape in the Del Mar is in the form of responsibly sourced leather. REEF uses Leather Working Group-certified leathers to ensure that its manufacturers are independently verified for sustainability. REEF also partners with organizations working to get more people out enjoying and protecting the ocean, including a partnership with The Mega Lab to map 1 million coral reefs by 2030. Additional partnerships with the Surfrider Foundation and Better Beach Alliance work to keep beaches clean and help preserve the planet. The Del Mar won’t replace your hiking boots or your dress shoes. That’s because it doesn’t want to. Instead, it covers the wide middle of the day. So when you’re moving between errands, hustling from meeting to meeting, or sneaking away from it all for a quick walk in the sun, you can do it in a shoe that looks as good as it feels. And that’s saying something. REEF believes life is better when it’s a little more effortless and a lot more comfortable. REEF builds products and stories for people who don’t overthink it, who move through life with ease, and who expect style to feel as good as it looks.

item.title: SALES: Go Further in Québec’s Winter Wilderness
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Let this sink in: More than 92 percent of Québec is public land. Come winter, those millions of acres of woods, trails, and open glades get absolutely buried in snow, turning the province into a sprawling winter playground where opportunities for ski touring, Nordic skiing, and multiday snowshoeing abound. All that wild landscape would be nothing without a trail system to match—which is why it’s a darn good thing that groomed trails and skintracks cover the province, courtesy of Québec’s adventure-minded culture and infrastructure. Cozy rustic huts dot the high country, Nordic centers pepper the lowlands, and there’s an extensive network of designated ski-touring areas across the region. Behind Québec’s extensive network of winter trails and refuges lies a long tradition of winter travel and exploration. Long before winter travel became a recreational pursuit, Indigenous peoples used snowshoes and knowledge passed down through generations to navigate the territory now known as Québec. Today, these snow-covered landscapes offer countless opportunities for exploration, from Nordic skiing and multi-day snowshoeing to backcountry adventures. Today, Québec boasts 28 national parks and dozens of Nordic and cross-country centers. It also boasts plenty of grassroots backcountry ski areas, each complete with trail maps and designated runs. There’s no avalanche mitigation at these sites—they’re wild at heart—but the effortless parking, signage, and basic infrastructure make them a perfect stepping stone between sidecountry and true backcountry. Always remember to come equipped with the appropriate training, equipment, and avalanche awareness. And if you’d rather explore with a qualified guide, you can find businesses certified through Aventure Écotourisme Québec’s Quality-Safety certification program, which sets recognized standards for risk management, guide training and service quality. Looking to do a little bit of everything? Try Vallée Bras-du-Nord. This all-season adventure center maintains both groomed cross-country ski trails and designated backcountry terrain. Its varied slopes and jaw-dropping views guarantee an unforgettable outing, while a collection of yurts and cabins make it a true ski-in, ski-out getaway. You won’t find a backcountry experience like it anywhere else in North America. For a more homegrown vibe, head to Sommets du Fjord, a blues-and-blacks zone just beyond the charming village of Petite-Saguenay. The town sits right on the edge of the legendary Saguenay Fjord National Park—yet another ski touring and snowshoeing epicenter—which makes it an ideal multisport base camp. Want to turn a great day into a great week? Treat yourself to a fully immersive multiday traverse through Québec’s snow-draped winter landscapes. Robust hut systems in national parks like Mont-Tremblant and Monts-Valins make it easy to plan linkups via Nordic ski or snowshoe, and village-to-village trips in the Laurentians like those along Les Routes Blanches offer chances to discover culture and cuisine alongside the stunning landscapes. Simply choose a trail to one or more of the parks’ remote refuges and use them as stopover points to cook, relax, and connect with your adventure buddies—and recharge by a blazing woodstove before hitting the trail again the next day. The adventure doesn’t end when the skis or snowshoes come off. Beyond the trails, Québec’s welcoming villages, local flavors, and cozy inns offer the perfect setting to unwind and reconnect. Share a well-earned meal, raise a glass of a local wine or brew with your fellow adventurers, and relive the day’s discoveries. Because sometimes, going further isn’t just about the distance you travel, it’s about everything you experience along the way. Your next winter adventure starts here. Whether you’re seeking powder-filled backcountry descents, multi-day Nordic ski routes or peaceful snowshoe expeditions through snow-covered forests, Québec invites you to explore further. Discover inspiring winter experiences and start planning your next expedition with Bonjour Québec.

item.title: SALES: Best online backup 2026: Expert reviews and top picks
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Online backup is your protection against any harm that might come to your computer or local storage devices. Mechanical failure, acts of malice, or natural disasters are serious threats to all of the data you have stored on your PC. While I always recommend keeping a local backup for quick restores (see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for desktop solutions), uploading your data to a cloud backup service is a good way to cover your bases. There’s a valid reason for the “backup rule of three,” which includes an offsite copy. Fortunately for consumers, there are myriad affordable and convenient online backup options, many with unique selling points. While my primary focus in this article is backup, I also discuss other roles that a cloud service can fulfill, such as document viewing and editing, file sharing, multiple-device support, and emergency-restore options. Note: You won’t see familiar names like Google Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox on this list. Those are more accurately defined as synced cloud storage. Besides typically lacking a desktop client, and offering limited, if any, automatic backup functionality, online storage syncing involves mirroring — where any deletions or changes are reflected on the other end. Online backup uses versioning, so older data is retained — an important failsafe feature. Why you should trust PCWorld for online backup reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name, PCWorld. Our reviewers have been testing PC hardware, software, and services for decades. Our backup evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the promises and limitations of every product — from performance to the practicalities of regular use. As PC users ourselves, we know what makes a product stand out. Only the best online backup services make this list. EaseUS Todo Backup – Cloud backup software EaseUS Todo Backup covers everything you need for backups, with great features and fair pricing. With free cloud storage space, you’ll always have an extra copy of any files stored securely in the cloud. Security Zone protects vital data from ransomware in real-time. - Supports multiple PCs and devices on the same account - Can back up Office 365, Google Workspace, and NAS - Needs better imaging and disaster recovery implementation Who should use iDrive? iDrive will satisfy most any user. It remains the most comprehensive online backup service I’ve tested. Though it’s not the cheapest, it’s still competitive price-wise and offers backup clients for nearly every PC/device operating system. The company also provides additional storage for syncing all your devices and PCs, allows sharing of files with anyone, has the ability to back up to a local drive, and supports basic imaging and disaster recovery. Since our last review, iDrive has expanded its backup offerings to cover a variety of personal and team needs. Besides the free 10GB tier, there’s a Personal plan that starts at 5TB/$69.65 for the first year (or $149.25 for two years), and $99.50 each year after, covering one user and multiple devices. Additional Personal tiers offer 10TB, 20TB, 50TB, and 100TB options, though of course with significant price increases. There are also Team plans that cover multiple users and multiple computers. - Syncing briefcase with online editing (Pro version) or separate service - Mac Client requires third-party software for briefcase functionality Who should use Livedrive? In my most recent look at Livedrive, I reviewer summed up the service up with one word: smooth. That’s really no surprise, as Livedrive’s elegant setup, ease of use, and reliability are the very things (along with unlimited storage) that made it one of my top picks for online backup over the last several years. There’s something very reassuring about using a product that is artfully designed and executed. But Livedrive should be of particular interest to anyone who wants the benefit of unlimited storage — the service’s real value proposition. Yes, Backblaze and Carbonite also offer unlimited storage, and are strong services in their own right, but there are caveats for both that push the highly polished Livedrive client ahead of them in my book. Currently, the standard Backup plan for one PC is approximately $124 per year (being a UK-based company, prices are listed in pounds and the conversion to dollars will fluctuate). A Pro Suite that covers five machines is $284 per year. Despite the servers being located “across the pond,” I experienced a brisk 5- to 10MBps upload rate from our base in San Francisco, CA, which should stave off any bandwidth worries for U.S.-based customers. OpenDrive – Best online backup for smaller data sets - Small operational inConsistencies between the Windows and macOS clients Who should use OpenDrive? OpenDrive offers a 500GB plan for $50 a year — which will cover a lot of users, and is just about the most affordable 1TB service these days at $60. In case you hadn’t noticed, most services have upped the price of admission recently. Case in point: OneDrive went from $70 to $120. And OpenDrive’s plans are full boat. A lot of services offer a super affordable first year that turns not so affordable after that. While the service doesn’t offer anything particularly fancy, there is both a local virtual drive à la Dropbox, etc and a client for backup jobs. The backup job is true backup where files are never overwritten. OpenDrive is also one of the most solid experiences I’ve had when it comes to operations and reliability. OpenDrive was also a very close contender for best online backup overall. A few more features and it could end up at the top of this list. - Online storage, multi-device sync, and mirroring - Fantastically affordable lifetime plans - Virtual drive integrates with Windows Explorer as a drive letter Who should use pCloud? For those desiring a feature-packed online backup solution that’s insanely affordable over time, pCloud is our current pick. Why? It offers some great lifetime plan: $199 for 500GB ($50 yearly), or $399 for 2TB ($100 yearly) and $1,190 for 10TB ($200 yearly). With many 1TB plans costing $80 to $100 or more a year (OneDrive is now $100), you’ll be saving money after only a few years. pCloud’s other neat trick is backing up from your other online accounts: Google Drive, OneDrive, Drop Box, and even Facebook. That’s a very handy end-user feature. As are the phone apps to back up your photos, etc. pCloud’s backup is actually two-way sync, but revisions are maintained for 15 to 180 days. A lifetime plan is only good while the company exists, but the Swiss-based firm has been around since 2013, so we expect continued solvency. Note that this is our standard caveat for any online storage/backup service offering lifetime plans. Note that OpenDrive (listed above), and Nordlocker vied for best budget distinction. There are also S3-compatible services that are very affordable if all you want to do with your online storage is to back up to it. Arq 7 Backup – Best for consolidating online storage - Backs up to and from a wide variety of third-party online storage services Who should use Arq 7? Anyone who leverages multiple storage services for backup will be interested in Arq 7, which allows you to create multiple jobs under one roof to upload and download from the majority of them. Supported services include Amazon, Google Drive and Cloud, OneDrive, Dropbox, BackBlaze B2, SFTP, S3-compatibles, some less known vendors such as pCloud, and more. The Arq 7 interface is easy-to-use and navigate, which is a huge boon considering how intimidating backing up to multiple services can be for new users. It’s also rather spartan; if you’re looking for bling, forget it. My only minor quibble with Arq 7 is that it’s a bit of a one-trick pony — only backing up. There are no perquisites such as partition or drive-image backups, cloning, recovery via boot media, such as those offered by iDrive. Not even sync is supported. If you only want to leverage your own existing online storage services, Arq 7 is available as a $49 standalone client with a perpetual license. With Arq’s own storage, it’s still only $6 a month, or $60 yearly for 1TB and five users. Still, backup is by far the most important task and Arq 7 does an excellent job of consolidating data to or from multiple online storage services. - Mac client not as responsive as it should be Who should use Icedrive? Icedrive offers both a free 10GB service and paid tiers. That’s 5GB more for free than with our former pick, Sync.com. The Icedrive web interface is both an attractive and easy to navigate, as is the client software (Windows, macOS, iOS, Linux, and Android). Said client software offers the same sync functions for free accounts as it does for paid tiers, which gives it a leg up over the free tiers of many other services. There’s also a local virtual drive à la Dropbox, Google Drive, and others. While 10GB of storage isn’t enough for power users or businesses, if you’re simply looking to keep documents online with the ability to sync them across multiple devices for free, Icedrive is a reliable service with an excellent client. Plus, you can always upgrade to a paid tier for more storage as needed. That might not be as pricey as you’d think, though the discounted prices on the site are for the first year only. Annually, Icedrive is $29 for 2TB (discounted from $99), $49 for 4TB (discounted from $159), and $99 for 6TB (marked down from $269). Most users will be best off with the 2TB plan which is quite competitive. Note that those discounted prices are for the first year only, reverting to full boat after that. Backup software with cloud backup/storage support Typically, we separate our reviews of cloud backup services from local backup software (as seen in our best Windows backup software roundup.) But those lines have been blurred with backup software that includes support for cloud backup and storage. The following are reviews of such hybrid offerings: - Handy Backup Professional: Top-notch features that might’ve garnered a higher rating had it been entirely glitch-free and a bit easier to learn. - Ashampoo Backup Pro 27: A great total backup solution for the average user, but a couple features shy of being “pro.” - Dropbox Backup: Dropbox Backup is a nice solution for one-person account users, despite surcharges for long-term version retention. - MSP360 Managed Backup: Backup for multiple computers at a decently low fee. Local and online, file-based and imaging, along with disaster recovery are all provided via manageable local clients. - R-Drive Image 7.3: This backup program has expanded support for cloud storage services — including the Amazon S3 and S3-compatible repositories - Iperius Backup Basic: This backup program offers power aplenty, but the learning curve and interface might occasionally flummox less-experienced users. - EaseUS ToDo Backup 2026: A full-featured program that ranks among the top; its free version is particular robust. - Zinstall FullBack: Unique among backup programs, it offers full migration of backed up data and apps to a new OS installation — for a relatively steep price. - Aomei Backupper Pro: A complete backup solution capable of preserving your important data both locally and remotely. - Aomei Backupper Standard: A respectable free backup program, if you can tolerate the occasional ad. It’s cloud storage is affordable but can only be used for backups, no other data. - Acronis True Image: Besides being feature-packed, including support for cloud backup storage, Acronis throws in protection against viruses and malware. - Retrospect 19 Solo: We like that this backup program includes support for both proprietary and third-party cloud storage, but not its lack of disaster recovery. - Retrospect 19 Desktop: The pro version to Solo’s consumer version, Retrospect Desktop covers all the bases, but has a steep learning curve and high price. Even local backup software that doesn’t offer a formal cloud component can be made to incorporate the most popular online storage services, using a cloud storage manager. The good news is that you have lots of options for putting together a comprehensive backup strategy including local and remote copies of all your data! How PCWorld tests and evaluates online backup services As noted above, the performance of online backup services will vary wildly according to their location and the network equipment between you and the data depository. We installed the software and backed up the same 2GB data set to check for any major issues or glitches in the client software. These are noted in the reviews. See our article on how PCWorld tests cloud backup services for all the details. Jon Jacobi has been dabbling in the computing arts since the days when that required flipping switches. He has witnessed data storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state drives. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. That necessarily includes the software and services that support data storage. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. How to pick an online storage and backup service Cloud backup has unique considerations. Familiarizing yourself with the following key areas can help you find the cloud backup service that best meets your needs. Obviously, you’ll need as much storage as you have data, plus a little, or possibly a lot, more if you want to track changes and save previous versions of files — if that’s supported. Some services keep multiple versions of files, some don’t. In many cases there’s a time limit. Nearly all online services charge differently depending on amount of storage involved. Uploads are free, but downloads may be limited. In some cases, there are upload and download charges. Read the fine print. Aside from the free tiers available from a service like Dropbox, pricing is fairly consistent across services, though you definitely get more capacity for your money from some vendors. As we mentioned previously, in addition to backup, you may want to share your files with others, work with them from mobile devices, or even edit them with office applications such as those available with Dropbox, Google, and OneDrive. If you do intend to work online, we recommend that you maintain a local copy as far-more-quickly-restored backup, as well as a hedge against Internet downtime. Most services provide client backup software for the major operating systems (Linux, OS X, and Windows) and both Android and iOS. Make sure the service you sign up for supports your entire panoply of computers and devices. If you’re concerned about the privacy of your data, make sure you use a service that allows the use of a personal encryption key that you define. Do NOT lose it, as it is absolutely required to restore your data. Sadly, using your own key often limits the types of services (e.g., no mobile backup) available. If private encryption keys aren’t available, read the privacy policy, especially with the free services—there are significant differences. What’s the best online backup? When it comes to the sheer volume of features, iDrive is the pick of the online backup litter. With honorable mentions to Livedrive for unlimited storage, and Sync.com for free storage with real backup features. What’s the best cheap online backup? Much of the “cheap” equation depends on how much storage you need. Icedrive in its 10GB free incarnation is PCWorld’s top pick for small amounts of data, with 5GB Sync.com next in freebie line. If you’re wondering why no OneDrive, Google Drive, etc. it’s because they don’t offer backup functions. Dropbox now offers a backup function (beta), so that’s another runner-up. Just avoid the Teams version of Dropbox Backup, which moves data before actually backing it up. For up to 1TB of storage, the lifetime deal of $199 from pCloud is hard to beat. How reliable is cloud backup? Generally speaking, data centers are backed up to the hilt, and some of the larger ones even back up to different geographical locations. Availability (hopefully 24/7) can also be important. Check for news of outages and the vendor’s own service blogs. All the services we’re aware of have been near-100 percent reliable. What speed and data transfer rates should I look for? Speed in most cases these days is far more dependent upon the speed of your broadband connection than that of the online service, though the geographical location of the storage and the equipment in between can make a significant difference. Check the location of the service’s data servers if speed is important to you. Or, just give the trial a whirl and see if you can live with it. How often should you schedule backups? Ideally, you should back up your data as often as possible. This is especially true if you are working on an important project or have data that you absolutely cannot afford to lose. It’s a good idea to automate the backup process and have the cloud service back up your data every hour or so. You might also consider real time (as files are changed), or continuous (more granular scheduling such as every 5 minutes.) Services such as Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are considered cloud storage services because they don’t offer local backup clients, but sync via a local virtual drive or web interface. A user must place their files onto the service’s cloud manually. A cloud backup service provides a desktop client with either versioning or retention of all the files you’ve backed up. Cloud backup service providers may also offer additional data security measures such as end-to-end encryption. Is it safe to store my data online? Yes! All cloud backup services offer encryption of your data both during the transfer to and from your computer as well as while your data is stored on the provider’s servers. While this encryption stops others from being able to view your data, it doesn’t necessarily stop them from stealing it. Generally speaking, while not infallible, cloud backup services are one of the most secure options for storing your data. Do you need to back up everything on your computer? You should at least back up all data that you can’t stand to lose. All devices will likely experience technical issues over time and oftentimes this leads to your data being lost from that device. So you should do regular backups of everything that is important to you. However, backup services typically offer more storage than most people can use, so it’s never a bad idea to safely store all of your data in case of emergency. What’s the difference between sync and backup? Though there can be variations such as one-way and mirroring, sync is generally thought of as any change (deletions included) to a data set reflected on all the data repositories involved in the sync. The change can be made in any repository and will propagate to the others. That includes the source, the online storage, and any devices linked to the account. Backup, on the other hand, should be an immutable copy of your source data from a point of time. In practice, however, vendors may use what’s known as versioning, i.e. retaining older copies of files while using the most recent version as the file shown in the backup. The effect is largely the same as incremental backup and requires a lot less time and space. Alas, when versioning or even plain backup are involved, there may be limits on how long older versions and deleted files are retained. This isn’t true backup, but simply a safer version of sync that allows vendors to reclaim space after a period of time. The good news? Most users won’t really need those older files. For those that do, be careful which service you choose.
